import typing as t

import fastapi
import fastapi.testclient
from pydantic import AliasChoices, BaseModel, Field


class Model(BaseModel):
    items: t.Annotated[list[str], Field(validation_alias=AliasChoices("items_alias", "items"))]


app = fastapi.FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def root(
    model: t.Annotated[Model, fastapi.Query()],
) -> Model:
    return model


client = fastapi.testclient.TestClient(app)


def request_with_params(params: dict):
    result = client.get("/", params=params)
    assert result.status_code == 200, (result.status_code, result.json())


request_with_params({"items": "asdf"})
request_with_params({"items_alias": ["asdf", "asd2"]})
request_with_params({"items_alias": "asdf"})  # <-- this one fails

I've created a Query-Model that contains a list field, so that the field may be provided in multiple times. I want to provide multiple aliases for this field. When I provide the field under the default name, all is well. When I provide multiple values under the alias, all is well. However, when I provide a single value under the alias, I get a validation error.
I would expect the validation to succeed with a single value under the alias name

discussions.title: Return type vs ORJSONResponse: does generic return type as dict[str, Any] use the Pydantic serializer efficently?
discussions.question_body:
First Check

 I added a very descriptive title here.
 I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
 I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
 I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
 I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Pydantic.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Swagger UI.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to ReDoc.

Commit to Help

 I commit to help with one of those options 👆

Example Code
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/example")
def example() -> dict[str, Any]:
return {"hello": "world"}
Description
Hi FastAPI team,
 
I have a question regarding the current response serialization behavior, especially after the recent ORJSONResponse deprecation guidance.
 
While investigating the warning:
 

FastAPI now serializes data directly to JSON bytes via Pydantic when a return type or response model is set
 
I inspected the implementation of fastapi.routing.serialize_response() in the version currently installed in my environment and found the following logic:
 

async def serialize_response(...):
if field:
...
serializer = field.serialize_json if dump_json else field.serialize
return serializer(...)
else:
return jsonable_encoder(response_content)
 
To better understand when the Pydantic serialization path is selected, I temporarily patched serialize_response() and logged the value of field during request execution.
 
For an endpoint defined only with a generic return type:
 
@app.get("/example")
def example() -> dict[str, Any]:
return {"hello": "world"}
 
the runtime output was:
 
ModelField(
field_info=FieldInfo(annotation=dict[str, Any], required=True),
name='Response_example',
mode='serialization',
config=None
)

 
This seems to indicate that FastAPI creates a response ModelField even for generic return types such as dict[str, Any], and therefore enters the field.serialize() path instead of the jsonable_encoder() path.
 
Based on this, I would like to confirm a few points:
 

Is this behavior intentional and considered part of the public/expected behavior of FastAPI?
 
Can users rely on a generic return type like:
 

-> dict[str, Any]
-> list[dict[str, Any]]
-> list[Any]
 
to activate the Pydantic response serialization path, even when no explicit response_model is provided?
 
3. From a performance perspective, should users generally prefer:
 
@app.get("/")
def endpoint() -> dict[str, Any]:
...
 
over:
 
@app.get("/", response_class=ORJSONResponse)
def endpoint():
...
 
given the current deprecation warning around ORJSONResponse?
 
4. Are there any meaningful performance differences between:
-> dict[str, Any]
 
and
 
-> MyPydanticModel
 
with regard to the generated serializer and serialization speed?
 
5. Would it be worth clarifying this point in the documentation?
 
The current wording mentions "return type or response model", which many readers (including me initially) could interpret as primarily referring to Pydantic models. However, from the implementation and runtime behavior it appears that even generic typed returns such as dict[str, Any] participate in the Pydantic serialization path.
 
Thanks for the clarification, and for all the work on FastAPI.
Operating System
Linux
Operating System Details
No response
FastAPI Version
0.140.7
Pydantic Version
2.13.4
Python Version
Python 3.13.0
Additional Context
No response
discussions.answer_body:
Your reading of the code is right. Numbers below are from your exact versions — FastAPI 0.140.7, Pydantic 2.13.4, Python 3.13.
1 and 2 — intentional, and yes you can rely on generics
Any return annotation FastAPI can build a TypeAdapter for produces a response field, generics included:
route annotation                  response_field  response_class  fast path
-> (none)                         none            default         False
-> dict[str, Any]                 yes             default         True
-> list[dict[str, Any]]           yes             default         True
-> list[Any]                      yes             default         True
-> Any                            yes             default         True
-> MyModel                        yes             default         True
-> dict[str, Any] + ORJSONResponse yes            ORJSON          False
-> (none) + ORJSONResponse        none            ORJSON          False

Even bare -> Any gets one. The only ways to end up on the jsonable_encoder branch are to omit the annotation or to return a Response object yourself.
3 — prefer the return type, and don't set both
This is the part worth knowing. From fastapi/routing.py in 0.140.7:
# Use the fast path (dump_json) when no custom response
# class was set and a response field with a TypeAdapter
# exists. Serializes directly to JSON bytes via Pydantic's
# Rust core, skipping the intermediate Python dict +
# json.dumps() step.
use_dump_json = response_field is not None and isinstance(
    response_class, DefaultPlaceholder
)
Passing response_class=ORJSONResponse means response_class is no longer a DefaultPlaceholder, so use_dump_json is False — you keep the response field but drop to field.serialize → Python objects → ORJSONResponse.render(). Setting both is the slowest of the three arrangements, not the fastest. (Both ORJSONResponse and UJSONResponse carry @deprecated in fastapi/responses.py, so the warning you hit is real, not advisory folklore.)
4 — a model is faster than dict[str, Any], and both beat the encoder path badly
Serialization only, 20,000 iterations, best of 3, 20-key flat dict with one nested value:
 4.9 us   -> MyModel                        serialize_json  (fast path)
 6.1 us   -> dict[str, Any]                 serialize_json  (fast path)
13.3 us   -> dict[str, Any]                 serialize + json.dumps
48.4 us   no annotation + ORJSONResponse    jsonable_encoder + orjson.dumps
53.8 us   no annotation                     jsonable_encoder + json.dumps
 0.8 us   orjson.dumps(payload)             raw, for reference

The model wins by roughly 25% because Any has no static schema — pydantic-core has to infer each value's type at runtime, while a declared model compiles a specialized serializer.
The bigger point is the ~8x gap to the encoder rows, and it explains the deprecation: the expensive part was never json.dumps vs orjson.dumps, it was jsonable_encoder walking the object graph in Python. That's also why ORJSONResponse only ever bought ~10% here — it optimized the cheap half of the work. Absolute numbers scale with payload size and shape; the ratios held across runs.
5 — agreed, worth documenting
"return type or response model" is accurate but reads as if it means Pydantic models specifically. Two additions would have saved you the source dive: that any return annotation qualifies, dict[str, Any] included, and that setting a custom response_class silently opts you out of the fast path. The second one is the surprising half — it's easy to assume the two optimizations stack. Happy to open a docs PR if a maintainer wants it.

discussions.title: jsonable_encoder drops exclude_defaults for dict values (propagated for list items)
discussions.question_body:
Summary
jsonable_encoder propagates exclude_defaults when recursing into list/tuple/set items, but silently drops it when recursing into dict values (and keys). The two sibling flags exclude_unset and exclude_none are forwarded in that same dict branch, so exclude_defaults is the lone omission. As a result the same Pydantic model, with the same flag, encodes differently depending on whether it sits inside a list or a dict.
Where
fastapi/encoders.py, dict branch value recursion:
encoded_value = jsonable_encoder(
    value,
    by_alias=by_alias,
    exclude_unset=exclude_unset,
    exclude_none=exclude_none,          # exclude_defaults is missing here
    custom_encoder=custom_encoder,
    sqlalchemy_safe=sqlalchemy_safe,
)
The list branch a few lines below passes exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults.
Reproduction (real fastapi.encoders.jsonable_encoder, pydantic 2.x)
from pydantic import BaseModel
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder

class M(BaseModel):
    a: int = 5
    b: int = 10

jsonable_encoder([M()], exclude_defaults=True)        # [{}]                     -> defaults stripped
jsonable_encoder({"k": M()}, exclude_defaults=True)   # {"k": {"a": 5, "b": 10}} -> NOT stripped
Same model, same flag, different result purely by container type.
Proposed fix
Add exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults to the dict-branch recursion (value, and for parity the key), matching the list branch and the two sibling flags already forwarded there:
encoded_value = jsonable_encoder(
    value,
    by_alias=by_alias,
    exclude_unset=exclude_unset,
    exclude_defaults=exclude_defaults,
    exclude_none=exclude_none,
    custom_encoder=custom_encoder,
    sqlalchemy_safe=sqlalchemy_safe,
)
Notes
exclude_defaults is a documented public parameter of jsonable_encoder. The default FastAPI response path calls it with exclude_defaults=False, so this doesn't affect default responses — it surfaces for direct jsonable_encoder(..., exclude_defaults=True) use (and internal callers passing the flag). Filing as a Discussion per the contributing guidelines — happy to open a PR with the one-line fix (and a test) if a maintainer would like.

First Check

 I added a very descriptive title here.

Commit to Help

Example Code
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

# custom error pydantic model that populate "detail" prop of (FastApi) HTTPException
# NOTE: this is a base class that need to be extended
class HttpExpectedError(BaseModel):
  code: str = Field(..., description="Error code like PLAYLIST_NOT_FOUND")
  message: str = Field(..., description="Error message for human")
  def toFastApiJson(self):
    return self.model_dump()

# concret error pydantic model for one route (that extends HttpExpectedError)
class HttpError_PlaylistNotFound(HttpExpectedError):
  code: Literal["PLAYLIST_NOT_FOUND"] = "PLAYLIST_NOT_FOUND"

# route
@app.get(
  path="/playlists/{playlist_id}",
  responses={
    404: {"model": HttpError_PlaylistNotFound}
  }
)
async def getOne():
  # ...
  if not playlist:
    raise HTTPException(
      status_code=404,
      detail=HttpError_PlaylistNotFound(
        message=f"Playlist {playlist_id} not found"
      ).toFastApiJson()
    )
Description
The code works, but:

the openapi spec schema (json) generated by FastApi and used by Docs UIs (swagger/scalar...) will make UIs think that JSON response would be:
{
  "code": "PLAYLIST_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "string"
}

...while the real returned JSON is:
{
  "detail": {
    "code": "PLAYLIST_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "string"
  }
}


The problem is the missing detail prop in the schema, how can i add it to the schema generated by fast api?

The contact.url only gets validated when the OpenAPI model is built, at OpenAPI(**output) at the end of openapi/utils.py. FastAPI() stores it as a raw dict at construction and builds the schema lazily on the first /openapi.json or /docs hit, then caches it, so nothing else trips over it first.
Want it to fail at startup? call app.openapi() once right after you construct the app. Same ValidationError on info.contact.url, just where the typo actually is. Checked on 0.115.0, unchanged on master.

Example Code
import os
import tempfile

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

dist = tempfile.mkdtemp()
with open(os.path.join(dist, "index.html"), "w") as f:
    f.write("<html>SPA shell</html>")

app = FastAPI()
app.frontend("/", directory=dist, fallback="index.html")

client = TestClient(app)

# The Accept header a browser sends on a normal top level navigation.
browser_nav = {
    "accept": "text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,"
    "image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,*/*;q=0.8"
}

print(client.get("/users/john", headers=browser_nav).status_code)      # 200, serves index.html
print(client.get("/users/john.doe", headers=browser_nav).status_code)  # 404
print(client.get("/v/1.2.3", headers=browser_nav).status_code)         # 404
Description
Hi 👋
I have been trying out the new app.frontend() helper to serve a single page app, using fallback="index.html" so that client side routes fall back to the shell and the frontend router can take over. This is the behavior described in the "Client side routing" part of the docs, and it works fine for a path like /dashboard or /dashboard/settings.
The problem shows up when a client side route has a dot in its last path segment. Plenty of real apps have these, for example a profile at /users/john.doe, a version deep link at /v/1.2.3, or a slug like /files/report.2024. When I open one of those directly, or just hit refresh while I am already on that page, I get a 404 instead of the index.html shell, so the app never loads and the client router never gets a chance to handle the route.
The part that surprised me is that setting fallback="index.html" explicitly does not change this. As far as I can tell there is currently no way to get these routes to fall back to the shell.
I spent some time reading the code and I think it comes from _is_frontend_navigation_request() in fastapi/routing.py. It takes the last path segment and if os.path.splitext(...) finds an extension it returns early and treats the request as an asset request, before it ever looks at the Accept header. Because os.path.splitext("john.doe") returns .doe, any segment with a dot in it is treated as a file and never gets the index.html fallback, even when the browser clearly asked for text/html.
What makes me think this is fixable without regressions is that the two situations are easy to tell apart. A real browser navigation sends Accept: text/html, while a missing asset requested from a script tag, an image tag, or a fetch call sends */* or a specific type like text/css. If I request a genuinely missing asset such as /assets/missing.js with Accept: */* it still returns 404 as expected, so checking the Accept header first would fix the navigation case and keep the asset case working.
I did notice there is already a test that pins the current behavior. test_index_fallback_does_not_handle_asset_like_or_non_html_requests has a ("/users/jane.doe", "text/html") case that expects a 404, so before proposing a change I wanted to ask whether the current behavior is intentional. If the idea is that dotted client routes should be servable, would a change that treats an explicit Accept: text/html request as navigation regardless of the path be acceptable? Or would you rather keep the extension heuristic as the default for fallback="auto" and add an opt in for apps that use dotted client side routes?
I am happy to open a PR with a failing test and the change for whichever direction you prefer. Thanks a lot for the work on this feature.

0.139.0
Pydantic Version
2.13.4
Python Version

No response

discussions.question_body:

Commit to Help

 I commit to help with one of those options 👆

Example Code
import asyncio
from fastapi.concurrency import contextmanager_in_threadpool


class TrackingCM:
    """Context manager that tracks whether __exit__ is called."""
    
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.exit_called = False
    
    def __enter__(self):
        print(f"  [{self.name}] __enter__ called")
        raise ValueError("setup failed")
    
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        self.exit_called = True
        print(f"  [{self.name}] __exit__ called  <-- PEP 343 violation!")


async def main():
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Behavioral inconsistency with Python context manager protocol")
    print("=" * 70)
    
    print("\n1. Standard Python `with`:")
    cm1 = TrackingCM("standard")
    try:
        with cm1:
            pass
    except ValueError:
        pass
    print(f"   Result: exit_called = {cm1.exit_called}")
    print(f"   OK: __exit__ NOT called when __enter__ raises")
    
    print("\n2. contextmanager_in_threadpool:")
    cm2 = TrackingCM("threadpool")
    try:
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm2):
            pass
    except ValueError:
        pass
    print(f"   Result: exit_called = {cm2.exit_called}")
    if cm2.exit_called:
        print(f"   FAIL: __exit__ IS called when __enter__ raises")
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 70)
    print("Root cause:")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("In fastapi/concurrency.py:")
    print("  try:")
    print("      yield await run_in_threadpool(cm.__enter__)  # if raises -> except")
    print("  except Exception as e:")
    print("      ok = bool(await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(cm.__exit__, ...))")
    print("")
    print("When __enter__ raises, the exception falls into `except`, and __exit__")
    print("is called. In standard Python `with`, if __enter__ raises, __exit__ is")
    print("NOT called (the context was never entered).")
    print("=" * 70)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
Description
I`m wrapping a sync context manager with contextmanager_in_threadpool. When enter raises, I expect exit to NOT be called, per PEP 343 (the context was never entered). Instead, exit IS called. See the Minimal Reproducible Example (MRE).
Operating System

discussions.answer_body:
Thanks for confirming this Sergei @yudin-s, and for the fix. Moving __enter__ out of the try fixes the first issue cleanly (and it also stops __exit__ swallowing the __enter__ exception when it returned True, which the old except block used to do).
I kept digging and found two more deviations from PEP 343 that the fix alone does not cover.
2. except Exception skips BaseException
The guard catches Exception but not BaseException. So KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, and asyncio.CancelledError raised in the body never reach __exit__. A standard with calls __exit__ for all of these:
class T:
    def __enter__(self): return self
    def __exit__(self, *a):
        print("exit called", a[0])
        return False

try:
    with T():
        raise KeyboardInterrupt()
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
# standard with: exit runs, receives KeyboardInterrupt
# contextmanager_in_threadpool: exit never runs
So the guard needs to be except BaseException.
3. Real anyio cancellation never reaches __exit__
This one is sneakier. Even with except BaseException, a real task cancellation (via cancel_scope.cancel()) still does not run __exit__. The await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...) call is itself a checkpoint: anyio sees the scope is still cancelled and re-raises CancelledError before the worker thread starts.
I confirmed this by canceling a task group child parked inside the context:
async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
    async def child():
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            await anyio.sleep(10)
    tg.start_soon(child)
    await anyio.sleep(0.1)
    tg.cancel_scope.cancel()
# cm.exit_called == False
That is the worst case for cleanup: cancellation is exactly when you want __exit__ to run, and it is exactly when it gets skipped.
4. The else (normal exit) branch has the same hole
The else branch runs __exit__(None, None, None) after a body that completed without raising. Its await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...) is a checkpoint too. If a cancel lands in the window between a checkpoint-free body returning and that await, __exit__ is skipped while __enter__ already ran - a straight resource leak. Reproducible:
async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
    async def child():
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            entered.set()   # body has no other await
    tg.start_soon(child)
    await entered.wait()
    tg.cancel_scope.cancel()
# without a shield on the else branch: cm.exit_called == False
# enter ran, exit did not
That window is narrow, but it is real. For a cleanup callback it should not exist at all.
Fix: shield every __exit__ thread call
exit_limiter = CapacityLimiter(1)
value = await run_in_threadpool(cm.__enter__)
try:
    yield value
except BaseException as e:
    with anyio.CancelScope(shield=True):
        ok = bool(
            await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(
                cm.__exit__, type(e), e, e.__traceback__, limiter=exit_limiter
            )
        )
    if not ok:
        raise
else:
    with anyio.CancelScope(shield=True):
        await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(
            cm.__exit__, None, None, None, limiter=exit_limiter
        )
Both __exit__ calls are now shielded. The mental model is simple: once __enter__ has run, __exit__ always runs to completion, cancellation or not. This mirrors what a synchronous with already does: __exit__ is a sync call, you cannot cancel it mid-flight.
Here are the tests that pin each of the cases above, so it is not just a claim. All run on both asyncio and trio (@pytest.mark.anyio), so the asyncio and trio variants are separate test items.
class EnterFailsCM:
    def __init__(self, exit_return: bool | None = False) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False
        self.exit_return = exit_return

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        raise ValueError("setup failed")

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool | None:
        self.exit_called = True
        return self.exit_return


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_enter_failure_does_not_call_exit() -> None:
    cm = EnterFailsCM()
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="setup failed"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            pass
    assert not cm.exit_called


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_enter_failure_propagates_even_if_exit_would_suppress() -> None:
    # old code: __exit__(True) would swallow the __enter__ ValueError
    cm = EnterFailsCM(exit_return=True)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="setup failed"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            pass
    assert not cm.exit_called


class ExitTrackingCM:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False
        self.exit_args: tuple = ()

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        return "value"

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool:
        self.exit_called = True
        self.exit_args = (exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb)
        return False


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_keyboard_interrupt_in_body_calls_exit() -> None:
    cm = ExitTrackingCM()
    with pytest.raises(KeyboardInterrupt, match="boom"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            raise KeyboardInterrupt("boom")
    assert cm.exit_called
    assert cm.exit_args[0] is KeyboardInterrupt


# SystemExit and manual asyncio.CancelledError are covered by two more tests
# of the same shape (test_system_exit_in_body_calls_exit,
# test_cancelled_error_in_body_calls_exit).


class SlowExitTrackingCM:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        return "value"

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool:
        self.exit_called = True
        return False


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_real_cancellation_still_calls_exit() -> None:
    import anyio

    cm = SlowExitTrackingCM()

    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        async def child() -> None:
            async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
                await anyio.sleep(10)

        tg.start_soon(child)
        await anyio.sleep(0.1)
        tg.cancel_scope.cancel()

    assert cm.exit_called


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_cancellation_after_normal_body_still_calls_exit() -> None:
    import anyio

    cm = SlowExitTrackingCM()
    entered = anyio.Event()

    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        async def child() -> None:
            async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
                entered.set()

        tg.start_soon(child)
        await entered.wait()
        tg.cancel_scope.cancel()

    assert cm.exit_called
The last test is the one that made me add the shield on the else branch too: without it, assert cm.exit_called fails on the asyncio backend (enter ran, exit did not). With the shield, it passes on both backends.
I have a full set of tests covering these cases locally. An earlier version went up as a PR but got closed/rejected, so I reworked it: the enter-out-of-try, the BaseException guard, and the shields on both branches are all pinned by tests now, on both asyncio and trio.
One tradeoff to flag: if __exit__ blocks (rollback to a dead DB), cancellation cannot interrupt it until __exit__ returns. That is the same constraint as a plain with, but it is worth being explicit about it.

discussions.title: Router-tree lazy rebuild (0.137.0+) is not thread-safe: valid routes can 404 under concurrent first requests
discussions.question_body:
First Check

 I added a very descriptive title here.
 I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
 I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
 I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
 I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Pydantic.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Swagger UI.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to ReDoc.

Commit to Help

 I commit to help with one of those options 👆

Example Code
"""Pure public API: N threads issue the app's FIRST requests concurrently,
each through its own TestClient (own event loop per thread). All requests
return 200 here, but the interleaved unlocked rebuilds leave the included
router's cached candidate list with far more than len(routes) entries —
permanently — and corrupt the global warnings filters. The same unlocked
window can also 404 valid routes (deterministic script in the description).
"""
import threading
import warnings

import fastapi
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

N_ROUTES = 120
N_THREADS = 6


def build_app() -> FastAPI:
    app = FastAPI()
    router = APIRouter()
    for i in range(N_ROUTES):
        def endpoint(q: int = 0, _i: int = i):
            return {"i": _i, "q": q}

        router.add_api_route(f"/r{i}", endpoint, methods=["GET"])
    app.include_router(router)
    return app


def main() -> int:
    print(f"fastapi {fastapi.__version__}")
    filters_before = len(warnings.filters)

    app = build_app()
    barrier = threading.Barrier(N_THREADS)
    statuses = []

    def worker() -> None:
        client = TestClient(app)
        barrier.wait()
        statuses.append(client.get(f"/r{N_ROUTES - 1}").status_code)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(N_THREADS)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    from fastapi.routing import _IncludedRouter

    included = next(r for r in app.router.routes if isinstance(r, _IncludedRouter))
    cache_len = len(included._effective_candidates)
    print(f"statuses: {statuses}")
    print(f"cached candidates: {cache_len} (expected {N_ROUTES})")
    if len(warnings.filters) != filters_before:
        print(f"warnings.filters leaked: {filters_before} -> {len(warnings.filters)}")
    return 1 if cache_len != N_ROUTES else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys

    sys.exit(main())
Description
Since the router-inclusion refactor in 0.137.0 (#15745), _IncludedRouter.effective_candidates() and effective_low_priority_routes() (fastapi/routing.py) rebuild their cached candidate lists lazily on first request with no synchronization:
routes_version = self.original_router._get_routes_version()
if routes_version == self._effective_candidates_version:   # (1) check
    return self._effective_candidates
self._effective_candidates = []                            # (2) wipe: publishes an EMPTY list on the shared attribute
...                                                        # (3) incremental self._effective_candidates.append(...)
self._effective_candidates_version = routes_version        # (4) stamp
(fastapi/routing.py:1583-1602 in 0.139.0; identical on current master.)
When more than one thread drives the same app object — e.g. a test suite whose worker threads each own a TestClient against one shared app, or any multi-loop/threaded embedding — the app's first concurrent requests race this rebuild. Three observable failures:
1. Spurious 404 on a valid route. A thread preempted between (1) and (2) that resumes after another thread completed (4) wipes a version-stamped cache. Until the wiper's own rebuild re-appends the tail routes, every request passes the check (1), iterates a half-built list, gets Match.NONE, and falls through to Router.default (await self.default(scope, receive, send), routing.py:2730) → bare 404 {'detail': 'Not Found'} for a perfectly valid path/method. We first noticed exactly this as intermittent 404s on an app's first requests in a real project's test suite (per-thread TestClients against one shared app).
2. Permanent candidate-cache corruption — the Example Code above; reproduces essentially every run. Concurrent rebuilds interleave their appends into the same last-assigned list, so the cache ends up with up to N_threads x N_routes entries. Typical output:
fastapi 0.139.0
statuses: [200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200]
cached candidates: 283 (expected 120)
warnings.filters leaked: 5 -> 6

(Observed 5/5 runs corrupted, counts varying with interleaving: 283, 166, 226, 247, 375.) Every subsequent request then iterates the duplicated candidates for the lifetime of the app.
3. Global warnings-filter corruption. The rebuild constructs pydantic TypeAdapters per route inside warnings.catch_warnings() (fastapi/_compat/v2.py, ModelField.__post_init__). catch_warnings mutates process-global state, so concurrent enter/exit corrupts warnings.filters — leaked filter entries (see output above) and UnsupportedFieldAttributeWarning escaping to stderr.
Deterministic reproduction of the 404
The 404 needs a specific preemption: between (1) and (2), across another thread's (4). This script forces exactly that schedule by pausing the first rebuilder at two legal preemption points with a threading.settrace hook — FastAPI code and behavior are untouched; the hook only makes an OS-schedulable interleaving reproducible. Three requests to the same valid route:

repro_404_deterministic.py
import inspect
import sys
import threading

import fastapi
import fastapi.routing as fastapi_routing
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI
from starlette.testclient import TestClient

N_ROUTES = 120


def build_app() -> FastAPI:
    app = FastAPI()
    router = APIRouter()
    for i in range(N_ROUTES):
        def endpoint(q: int = 0, _i: int = i):
            return {"i": _i, "q": q}

        router.add_api_route(f"/r{i}", endpoint, methods=["GET"])
    app.include_router(router)
    return app


def find_lines() -> tuple:
    func = fastapi_routing._IncludedRouter.effective_candidates
    lines, start = inspect.getsourcelines(func)
    wipe = append = None
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        if "_effective_candidates = []" in line:
            wipe = start + i
        if "_effective_candidates.append(route_context)" in line:
            append = start + i
    if wipe is None or append is None:
        raise AssertionError("lines not found - fastapi internals changed?")
    return func.__code__, wipe, append


CODE, WIPE_LINE, APPEND_LINE = find_lines()
victim_parked = threading.Event()       # victim sits between check (1) and wipe (2)
victim_release = threading.Event()
victim_mid_rebuild = threading.Event()  # victim wiped + appended <=1 entry
victim_finish = threading.Event()
_parked_once = False
_parked_mid = False
_victim_ident = None


def install_schedule_points() -> None:
    """Two legal preemption points for the FIRST thread that rebuilds (the
    'victim'; both apply to that same thread only). The ASGI app runs on anyio
    portal threads spawned by each TestClient, so we key on 'first arriver'."""

    def local_trace(frame, event, arg):
        global _parked_once, _parked_mid, _victim_ident
        if event == "line":
            if frame.f_lineno == WIPE_LINE and not _parked_once:
                _parked_once = True
                _victim_ident = threading.get_ident()
                victim_parked.set()
                victim_release.wait()   # P1: parked exactly between (1) and (2)
            elif (
                frame.f_lineno == APPEND_LINE
                and threading.get_ident() == _victim_ident
                and not _parked_mid
            ):
                _parked_mid = True
                victim_mid_rebuild.set()
                victim_finish.wait()    # P2: wiped, list nearly empty
        return local_trace

    def global_trace(frame, event, arg):
        if frame.f_code is CODE:
            return local_trace
        return None

    threading.settrace(global_trace)


def main() -> int:
    print(f"fastapi {fastapi.__version__}, python {sys.version.split()[0]}")
    app = build_app()
    target = f"/r{N_ROUTES - 1}"  # a perfectly valid route
    statuses = {}

    install_schedule_points()

    def request(name: str) -> None:
        client = TestClient(app)  # own event loop per thread
        r = client.get(target)
        statuses[name] = (r.status_code, r.json())

    victim = threading.Thread(target=request, args=("victim",), name="victim")
    victim.start()
    assert victim_parked.wait(timeout=30), "victim never reached the wipe line"

    # While the victim sits between (1) and (2): a normal request fully
    # builds the cache and stamps the version.
    warmer = threading.Thread(target=request, args=("warmer",), name="warmer")
    warmer.start()
    warmer.join()
    included = next(
        r for r in app.router.routes
        if isinstance(r, fastapi_routing._IncludedRouter)
    )
    assert statuses["warmer"][0] == 200, statuses["warmer"]
    assert included._effective_candidates_version is not None, "cache not stamped"
    assert len(included._effective_candidates) == N_ROUTES

    # Release the victim: its very next bytecode wipes the stamped cache.
    # It is paused again (P2) right at the first append of its rebuild loop.
    victim_release.set()
    assert victim_mid_rebuild.wait(timeout=30), "victim never reached the append line"
    assert len(included._effective_candidates) <= 1, "wipe did not land as scheduled"
    assert included._effective_candidates_version is not None  # version still stamped!

    # A third, completely ordinary request: version check passes, list is
    # half-built -> falls through to Router.default -> 404.
    reader = threading.Thread(target=request, args=("reader",), name="reader")
    reader.start()
    reader.join()

    victim_finish.set()
    victim.join()

    for name in ("warmer", "victim", "reader"):
        print(f"{name:>7}: {statuses[name]}")

    ok = (
        statuses["warmer"][0] == 200
        and statuses["victim"][0] == 200
        and statuses["reader"][0] == 404
    )
    if ok:
        print(f"\nBUG REPRODUCED: valid route {target} returned 404 after the "
              "version-stamped candidate cache was wiped by a concurrently "
              "rebuilding thread.")
        return 1
    print("\nschedule did not produce the 404 (unexpected)")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Output (identical on a pristine pip install fastapi httpx venv):
fastapi 0.139.0, python 3.12.13
 warmer: (200, {'i': 119, 'q': 0})
 victim: (200, {'i': 119, 'q': 0})
 reader: (404, {'detail': 'Not Found'})

BUG REPRODUCED: valid route /r119 returned 404 after the version-stamped
candidate cache was wiped by a concurrently rebuilding thread.

Under plain concurrent load the same window is hit stochastically (CPU load increases the rate); the Example Code shows the underlying interleaving happens essentially every time, so hitting the 404 in the wild is a matter of scheduling luck, not of whether the race exists.
Who is exposed
A single-event-loop server (typical uvicorn worker) matches routes on one thread, so it does not contend on the rebuild. Exposed are setups where one app object is driven from multiple threads/loops: parallel test suites with per-thread TestClients, threaded/multi-loop embeddings, apps shared across loops.
Suggested fix
Build into a local list and publish only when complete, stamping after publishing; concurrent rebuilds then become redundant but harmless:
def effective_candidates(self):
    routes_version = self.original_router._get_routes_version()
    if routes_version == self._effective_candidates_version:
        return self._effective_candidates
    candidates: list[_EffectiveRouteContext | _IncludedRouter] = []
    for route in self.original_router.routes:
        ...  # append to the local `candidates`
    self._effective_candidates = candidates
    self._effective_candidates_version = routes_version
    return candidates
Same pattern for effective_low_priority_routes(). A threading.Lock would also close the window and additionally serialize the redundant rebuild work; the local-build variant relies on CPython attribute-store atomicity, so free-threaded builds may still want the lock. Note that the warnings.catch_warnings() usage in ModelField.__post_init__ stays inherently thread-unsafe whenever model fields are built at request time — even with the rebuild race fixed, two loops building adapters concurrently can still corrupt the global filters; that may deserve a separate look.
Affected versions
Introduced with the router-tree refactor #15745 in 0.137.0 (verified: 0.136.0 has no _IncludedRouter; 0.137.0 has the identical unlocked pattern). Reproduced on 0.139.0 (current latest); the code is unchanged on current master. Also relevant: starlette 1.3.1, httpx 0.28.1, anyio 4.14.1.

Description

Create a new FastAPI environment e.g. with uv via the following

uv init .
echo "3.14.0" > .python-version
uv python install
uv add "fastapi[standard]"


Run the example code via uv run fastapi dev.
FastAPI immediately segfaults:

❯ uv run fastapi dev --verbose
 ~/Programmieren/fastapi-segfault  main ?6                                                                  SEGV ✘  3.14.0    14:49:26

If I switch to Python 3.13, it works fine.

macOS

discussions.answer_body:
Look at the path in your  faulthandler output:
/Users/philip/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.14.0a6-macos-x86_64-none/lib/python3.14/...

That's not Python 3.14.0 final... it's 3.14.0 alpha 6 (a6). Even though your .python-version says 3.14.0 and uv python install ran without complaint, uv resolved to a stale alpha build it had cached from earlier in the 3.14 beta cycle, rather than downloading the actual final release. This is a known uv quirk. There are several open uv issues describing exactly this (astral-sh/uv#13361, #18414): a previously installed pre release CPython build gets reused/resolved instead of the version you asked for.
That fully explains the segfault. CPython alpha/beta builds are not ABI-stable... internal struct layouts can and do change between alpha6 and the final 3.14.0 release. pydantic-core (and friends like uvloop/watchfiles) ship compiled wheels built against the final 3.14 ABI. Load one of those into an alpha6 interpreter and you get a silent, traceback less SEGV - which is exactly what you saw, and exactly why it crashes deep inside pydantic-core's class-creation code for Secret (that's the kind of code that touches CPython internals most directly).
Fix:
uv python list                      # confirm you have a stray cpython-3.14.0a6-... entry
uv python uninstall 3.14.0a6        # remove the alpha build
rm -rf .venv
uv python install 3.14.0            # explicit, full final version
uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"   # confirm it says 3.14.0, NOT 3.14.0a6
uv sync
uv run fastapi dev
If uv python list still offers the alpha as the resolved match for 3.14.0, that's a uv bug worth reporting on astral-sh/uv directly... but it isn't a FastAPI or Pydantic bug.

discussions.title: app.routes contains _IncludedRouter with no .path since 0.137
discussions.question_body:
Since 0.137, app.routes can contain _IncludedRouter objects that have no .path attribute. Code that iterates app.routes and reads route.path worked on earlier versions and now raises AttributeError.
from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter

sub = APIRouter()

@sub.get("/items")
def items():
    return {}

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(sub, prefix="/v1")

[route.path for route in app.routes]
# AttributeError: '_IncludedRouter' object has no attribute 'path'
Before 0.137, include_router copied each child route into app.routes, so every entry exposed .path. Now it appends a single _IncludedRouter that matches lazily and has no .path. On a CORS preflight (path matches, method doesn't) it returns a partial match, and a consumer that reads .path on the matched route raises.
This has hit a few tools that read .path off app.routes:

opentelemetry-instrumentation-fastapi reads route.path on a partial match; this took down our preflights in production (every browser OPTIONS to the API 500'd with no CORS header)
trallnag/prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator#370
vllm-project/vllm#45597

Would you want _IncludedRouter to expose .path (the include prefix), matching Route/Mount/Host, or handle it another way? Happy to send a PR.

from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter

leaf = APIRouter()

@leaf.get("")                                # empty path

It only happens when an empty-path route (path="") is nested and at least one include hop in its ancestry has no prefix. If every hop carries a prefix it still works on 0.137.0. Verified on both versions:

0.137.0

works


inner and app both include with a prefix

Root-cause pointer (from a quick read of 0.137.0 fastapi/routing.py): in include_router, when prefix is empty, it recursively iterates the included route candidates and raises if any route's raw path is empty — without composing the prefixes contributed by the intermediate included routers.
So a leaf that was included with a prefix at an inner hop still trips the check at a prefix-less outer include.
Whether the right fix is to validate the effective (prefix-composed) path, or to defer this validation to route-resolution time, is a design call for the refactor author.

discussions.title: 0.137.0: `APIRoute.tags` invisible to type checkers in generate_unique_id_function (regression from #15745)
discussions.question_body:
First check

I searched existing discussions and issues — no existing report for this.
This is about a type-checker regression in 0.137.0, not a runtime bug (runtime is unaffected).

Summary
In 0.137.0, the documented generate_unique_id_function pattern from Advanced → Generate Clients — which reads route.tags — now fails static type checking. Type checkers report that APIRoute has no attribute tags, even though the docs still show exactly this code and it works fine at runtime.
This appears to be an unintended side-effect of #15745 ("Refactor internals to preserve APIRouter and APIRoute instances"): APIRoute.__init__ was changed to delegate state-setting to a helper that receives self cast to the _APIRouteLike Protocol, and APIRoute itself no longer carries a class-level tags annotation. So the attribute is still assigned at runtime, but it's invisible to type checkers looking at the APIRoute type.
Reproducible example
This is the docs' own example (docs_src/generate_clients/tutorial003_py310.py):
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.routing import APIRoute


def custom_generate_unique_id(route: APIRoute) -> str:
    return f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}"


app = FastAPI(generate_unique_id_function=custom_generate_unique_id)
Running a type checker (ty) over it on 0.137.0:
error[unresolved-attribute]: Object of type `APIRoute` has no attribute `tags`
 --> repro.py:6:15
  |
6 |     return f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}"
  |               ^^^^^^^^^^

At runtime the same code builds the app and generates operation IDs correctly — only the static type surface is affected. route.name resolves fine; only route.tags is missing.
Expected behavior
route.tags should remain visible to type checkers as a public attribute of APIRoute (it's part of the documented public callback contract), as it was in 0.136.x where APIRoute.__init__ assigned self.tags = tags or [] directly.
Environment

FastAPI: 0.137.0
Python: 3.14
Type checker: ty 0.0.49 (also reproduces with strict Pyright per the same root cause); mypy may differ
OS: macOS

Possible fix
Add the lost class-level annotation back to APIRoute (e.g. tags: list[str | Enum]) so it matches what the _APIRouteLike Protocol already declares. Happy to open a PR if that direction is welcome.
Thanks for FastAPI! 🙏

Example Code
import sys, pytest
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr
from fastapi import FastAPI, Form
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

class Ce(BaseModel): 
  x: EmailStr | None = Field(None, min_length=6)

app = FastAPI()

@app.post('/post')
async def post(ce: Ce = Form()):

    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json()  == {'x': None}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(pytest.main())
Description
I try to model a Html Form that has an optional email field.
The intention is to have it  either be absent or validate with the properties set.
The pydantic model
class Ce(BaseModel): 
  x: EmailStr | None = Field(None, min_length=6)

works for manually instantiating a model, but fails when done via a HTML Form Post where the form has the email input not filled out.
It seems in this case, broswers send this datum as emty-string, such that not providing an email tries to instantiate the model as if it would be Ce(x="").
Can I remedy that besides making "" the default for the EmailStr field?
I wanto model an optional email address.
(Expanded version of code here)
Operating System
Linux, macOS
Operating System Details
No response
FastAPI Version
0.136.3
Pydantic Version
2.13.4
Python Version
Python 3.14.5
Additional Context
No response
discussions.answer_body:
Because HTML browsers submit empty form inputs as an empty string ("") rather than omitting them or sending null, Pydantic attempts to validate "" against your EmailStr and min_length constraints, resulting in a validation error.
The best solution is to use Pydantic's BeforeValidator to intercept the data before standard validation runs, converting any empty string into None.
If you apply constraints like min_length at the top level of the Annotated type (e.g. Field(min_length=6)), Pydantic will attempt to apply the constraint to None values as well. This leads to a TypeError (e.g., object of type 'NoneType' has no len()).
To prevent this, the constraint should be nested inside the EmailStr member of the Union type. This ensures that the length constraint is only evaluated when the value is a string.
Solution using a nested reusable Annotated type
You can create a reusable pre-validator function and combine it with Annotated to define a custom type. This keeps your models clean and allows you to reuse the logic across multiple optional form fields.
import sys
from typing import Annotated
import pytest
from fastapi import FastAPI, Form
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel, BeforeValidator, EmailStr, Field


# 1. Create a reusable function to transform empty strings to None
def empty_to_none(v: any) -> any:
    return None if v == "" else v


# 2. Define a reusable Annotated type
# The min_length constraint is nested specifically inside the EmailStr type definition
OptionalEmail = Annotated[
    Annotated[EmailStr, Field(min_length=6)] | None, BeforeValidator(empty_to_none)
]


class Ce(BaseModel):
    # Use your clean, reusable type here
    x: OptionalEmail = None


app = FastAPI()


# FastAPI automatically parses incoming form fields into the Pydantic model
@app.post("/post")
async def post(ce: Ce = Form()):
    return ce


# --- Test Suite ---

client = TestClient(app)


def test_write_noneok():
    # Case 1: Field is entirely absent from the form submission
    response = client.post("/post", data={})
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {"x": None}


def test_write_emptyok():
    # Case 2: Field is present but empty (browser default behavior)
    response = client.post("/post", data={"x": ""})
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {"x": None}


def test_write_valid_email():
    # Case 3: Field has valid data
    response = client.post("/post", data={"x": "user@example.com"})
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {"x": "user@example.com"}


def test_write_invalid_email():
    # Case 4: Field has invalid data (fails min_length or EmailStr)
    response = client.post("/post", data={"x": "a@b"})
    assert response.status_code == 422  # Validation Error


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(pytest.main([__file__]))

discussions.question_body:
First Check

 I added a very descriptive title here.
 I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
 I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
 I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
 I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.

 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Swagger UI.

Commit to Help

 I commit to help with one of those options 👆

Example Code
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()

# Counts how many times the non-cached child actually runs.
child_run_count = 0


def child_dependency() -> int:  # non-cached child (use_cache=False below)
    global child_run_count
    child_run_count += 1
    return child_run_count


def cached_parent(  # cached parent (use_cache=True by default)
    value: int = Depends(child_dependency, use_cache=False),
) -> int:
    return value


@app.get("/example")
def example(
    # The SAME cached parent dependency is requested twice.
    first: int = Depends(cached_parent),
    second: int = Depends(cached_parent),
):
    return {"first": first, "second": second, "child_run_count": child_run_count}


client = TestClient(app)
print(client.get("/example").json())
# Currently prints: {'first': 1, 'second': 1, 'child_run_count': 2}
Description
When a cached dependency is used more than once in a request, FastAPI currently re-solves its whole tree of sub-dependencies every time and then just discards that work away because the result is already in the cache. This PR skips that wasted work.
Today
For each dependency, solve_dependencies always recurses and solves the entire sub-tree first, and only afterwards checks the cache. If the value is already cached, all of that work is discarded.
So a use_cache=True dependency that's used twice in a request gets its sub-tree solved twice, even though only the first result is kept.
Example
cached_parent is cached and used twice. It depends on child_dependency, which is not cached:
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()
child_run_count = 0


def child_dependency() -> int:  # non-cached child
    global child_run_count
    child_run_count += 1
    return child_run_count


def cached_parent(  # cached parent (use_cache=True by default)
    value: int = Depends(child_dependency, use_cache=False),
) -> int:
    return value


@app.get("/example")
def example(
    first: int = Depends(cached_parent),
    second: int = Depends(cached_parent),
):
    return {"first": first, "second": second, "child_run_count": child_run_count}


print(TestClient(app).get("/example").json())

Today: {'first': 1, 'second': 1, 'child_run_count': 2} — cached_parent runs once (correct), but child_dependency runs twice. The second run happens only because the cached parent's sub-tree is re-walked; its result is then discarded, since cached_parent returns its cached value and never uses it.
With this PR: {'first': 1, 'second': 1, 'child_run_count': 1} — the cached parent is reused without re-solving its sub-tree, so child_dependency runs once.

Potential fix
Check the cache before recursing, and reuse the value if it's already there:
if sub_dependant.use_cache and sub_dependant.cache_key in dependency_cache:
    solved = dependency_cache[sub_dependant.cache_key]
    if sub_dependant.name is not None:
        values[sub_dependant.name] = solved
    continue
A value only lands in the cache after it has been solved successfully, so a cache hit means re-solving would just produce the same result. With this early check in place, the old cache check that ran after recursing is no longer reachable, so it's removed.

from fastapi import Body, FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType


class Cat(BaseModel):

    barks: float


class Lizard(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["reptile", "lizard"]
    scales: bool


Pet = TypeAliasType(
    "Pet",
    Annotated[Cat | Dog | Lizard, Field(discriminator="pet_type")],
)


bare_app = FastAPI(title="Bare Pet Example")


@bare_app.post("/pets")
def create_bare_pet(pet: Pet):
    return pet


@bare_app.get("/debug-openapi")
def debug_bare_openapi():
    schema = bare_app.openapi()
    request_schema = schema["paths"]["/pets"]["post"]["requestBody"]["content"][
        "application/json"
    ]["schema"]

    return {
        "request_schema": request_schema,
        "components": list(schema.get("components", {}).get("schemas", {}).keys()),
    }


body_app = FastAPI(title="Body Pet Example")


@body_app.post("/pets")
def create_body_pet(pet: Annotated[Pet, Body()]):
    return pet


@body_app.get("/debug-openapi")
def debug_body_openapi():
    schema = body_app.openapi()
    request_schema = schema["paths"]["/pets"]["post"]["requestBody"]["content"][
        "application/json"
    ]["schema"]

    return {
        "request_schema": request_schema,
        "components": list(schema.get("components", {}).get("schemas", {}).keys()),
    }


app = FastAPI(title="Compare TypeAliasType OpenAPI Behavior")
app.mount("/bare-case", bare_app)
app.mount("/body-case", body_app)
Description
I wanted to check whether this OpenAPI behavior is expected before opening an issue or PR.
I am using a named Pydantic TypeAliasType for a top-level discriminated union request body. Runtime validation works correctly in both cases, but the generated OpenAPI differs depending on whether the parameter is written as a bare annotation or explicitly wrapped with Body().
This came up while looking at this Pydantic issue: pydantic/pydantic#13236
My understanding from that discussion is that Pydantic validation/schema generation is working, and that the remaining discrepancy may be in FastAPI’s OpenAPI/request-body handling.
I also searched for related FastAPI issues/discussions and found #10719, #12149, #13635, and #13920, which seem related to FastAPI’s handling of PEP 695 / TypeAliasType aliases with Annotated metadata. Those appear to be addressed by #13920. I am using FastAPI 0.136.1, so this should include those fixes, but this specific OpenAPI component behavior still reproduces.
Run the example with:
uvicorn main:app --reload
Then open:
http://127.0.0.1:8000/bare-case/debug-openapi
http://127.0.0.1:8000/body-case/debug-openapi
http://127.0.0.1:8000/bare-case/docs
http://127.0.0.1:8000/body-case/docs

With the bare annotation:
@bare_app.post("/pets")
def create_bare_pet(pet: Pet):
    return pet
FastAPI emits the request body schema inline:
{
  "oneOf": [
    {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Cat"},
    {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Dog"},
    {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Lizard"}
  ],
  "title": "Pet",
  "discriminator": {
    "propertyName": "pet_type",
    "mapping": {
      "cat": "#/components/schemas/Cat",
      "dog": "#/components/schemas/Dog",
      "reptile": "#/components/schemas/Lizard",
      "lizard": "#/components/schemas/Lizard"
    }
  }
}
The generated components do not include Pet:
["Cat", "Dog", "HTTPValidationError", "Lizard", "ValidationError"]

With the explicit Body() annotation:
@body_app.post("/pets")
def create_body_pet(pet: Annotated[Pet, Body()]):
    return pet
FastAPI emits:
{"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Pet"}
and the generated components include Pet:
["Cat", "Dog", "HTTPValidationError", "Lizard", "Pet", "ValidationError"]

I also confirmed visually in Swagger UI that /bare-case/docs does not show a reusable Pet schema under Schemas, while /body-case/docs does.
Both route parameters represent the same logical request body type:
Pet = TypeAliasType(
    "Pet",
    Annotated[Cat | Dog | Lizard, Field(discriminator="pet_type")],
)
The bare annotation validates correctly, and the inline schema has the correct title, oneOf, and discriminator metadata. However, only Annotated[Pet, Body()] preserves the named alias as a reusable OpenAPI component.
My question: Is this expected behavior?
Would it make sense for FastAPI to preserve the named schema component for a bare named Pydantic TypeAliasType request body, matching the Annotated[Pet, Body()] behavior?
If this is considered valid behavior to align, I would be happy to contribute a focused regression test or small PR.

discussions.title: format_sse_event() does not validate event/id fields, allowing SSE protocol injection
discussions.question_body:
Problem
PR #15588 added validation to ServerSentEvent so that multi-line values for event and id are rejected. However, the public format_sse_event() function in fastapi.sse does not apply those same checks.
This means a caller who passes user-supplied data directly to format_sse_event() can unintentionally inject arbitrary SSE fields:
from fastapi.sse import format_sse_event

# attacker-controlled input
format_sse_event(event="legit\ndata: injected", data_str="safe")
# produces: b'event: legit\ndata: injected\ndata: safe\n\n'
The extra data: injected line was never intended — it is a protocol injection caused by the missing newline check.
Proposed fix
Reuse the existing _check_event_single_line and _check_id_valid helpers at the top of format_sse_event, the same way ServerSentEvent uses them. This makes both entry points enforce identical rules.
The change is two lines added to fastapi/sse.py and eight new parametrised tests in tests/test_sse.py (covering \n, \r, \r\n, and \0). All existing tests continue to pass.
Question
Would a PR with this fix be welcome?

discussions.title: Should commercial deploy tooling ship by default in the `[standard]` extra?
discussions.question_body:
Hi Sebastián and team,
I want to raise an ergonomic / supply-chain-hygiene question about a change in fastapi 0.136.3, not as a complaint about the underlying choice but as feedback on how it lands for downstream maintainers and security tooling. I'm a fastapi user shipping a framework that depends on fastapi transitively.
Context
In 0.136.3, the [standard] extras group gained two transitive deps via fastapi-cli[standard] → fastapi-cloud-cli:

fastar>=0.9.0 — Rust tar bindings, used by fastapi-cloud-cli/commands/deploy.py:127 to write zstd-compressed tarballs for cloud upload. Completely legitimate; the name is fast+tar.
sentry-sdk, rignore, etc. — telemetry + Rust-backed gitignore parsing for the deploy flow.

pyproject.toml cleanly declares both standard and the new standard-no-fastapi-cloud-cli extras — so opt-out exists for users who want it, which I appreciate.
What's happened downstream
The Amazon Inspector vulnerability database has issued advisory MAL-2026-4750 flagging 0.136.3 as a malicious release. The advisory's substantive claims are wrong (fastar is not a typosquat, the dep has a legitimate purpose, the opt-out extra demonstrates intentional design), but pip-audit + similar tooling propagate the finding to every project that resolves fastapi==0.136.3. As of writing, every downstream project running pip-audit --strict in CI is red-blocked. The advisory will probably be retracted eventually, but in the meantime maintainers across the ecosystem are pinning !=0.136.3 defensively.
That's not your responsibility to fix and I don't think you owe anyone a response to it. But it surfaces a real ergonomic question that I think is worth a conversation:
The actual question
The canonical install doc still says pip install "fastapi[standard]". With 0.136.3, this:

Adds commercial-deploy tooling (fastapi-cloud-cli → FastAPI Cloud) to the default-recommended install path.
Pulls in Rust-backed deps with single-maintainer authorship (fastar, rignore).
Adds outbound-network telemetry (sentry-sdk).

The opt-out extra (standard-no-fastapi-cloud-cli) exists, which is great — but it requires users to (a) know the cloud-cli is now bundled, (b) know they don't want it, and (c) remember to type a much longer extras name. Most users following the official docs will install the full [standard].
Would the team consider one of these?

(A) Promote standard-no-fastapi-cloud-cli (perhaps under a shorter name like serve or core-standard) to be the primary recommended install, with [standard] opt-in for cloud-cli users.
(B) Leave the resolution as-is but add a clearer call-out in the [standard] install docs that it now bundles commercial deploy tooling, with a one-liner pointer to the opt-out extra.
(C) Move fastar and the other cloud-cli-specific transitive deps so they're declared in fastapi-cloud-cli's own [standard] (which they are, currently) but not re-declared in fastapi's [standard] — i.e. let users get them only when they install fastapi-cli[standard] explicitly. (This may already be the structure; I haven't fully traced it.)

None of these is urgent. The current shape is defensible — I'm only flagging the question because a lot of downstream maintainers got a confusing CI red today, and the trajectory of "framework's recommended install path silently grows commercial tooling" is worth a moment of explicit thought even if the outcome is "yes, that's the trade-off we're making."
Thanks for fastapi. Happy to provide more context on the pip-audit failure path if useful.
discussions.answer_body:
Thanks for the comment!
About the false positive from Amazon, more of the context is here: ossf/malicious-packages#1274 , it seems it was an automated AI scan that reported a vulnerability, got accepted, created a CVE, etc. without ever even attempting to contact us. 🥲  But they are withdrawing it now.
About single-maintainer dependencies, that's how most of the entire open source ecosystem works, in most cases works fine, and in most cases there's one specific person (or a very small few) leading a project, that's not really an issue. The fact that it's under a person's username also doesn't limit permissions to maintain, they could add extra people. Same with an org, the fact that it's an org doesn't necessarily change things, it could still be a single person leading.
About the default standard dependencies, your option C is what already is in place, sadly, the automated detection didn't even check that.
About how to explain what is installed and done, we do that profusely, it's in the docs, sadly there's no easy way to explain more than that. We don't have a direct channel with users, not even telemetry. Sentry is installed for the cloud CLI for when there are errors deploying, but that's not activated when running the regular FastAPI commands. It would be very useful to know what things people use and what not, to be able to deprecate things, but we don't do that as that would raise concerns, it's only for cloud users.
The current decision to make those things part of standard is that that is the standard experience I would think users could get by default:

It is designed to be the default, official, and simplest way to deploy FastAPI to the cloud. Anyone can deploy it to any other platform, but that is the one made by and for FastAPI.
The default is made to be the one with the lowest friction, if a user needs to perform a bunch of additional steps just to get the recommended experience of deploying, then it's not as straightforward as it should it, which is also the spirit of FastAPI in general, to have good defaults on. Important in particular to newcomers to FastAPI and Python.
It is already opt-in, people have to install "fastapi[standard]" to get that plus the other things (e.g. uvloop and httptools for high performance). But if they simply install fastapi, they won't get any of that.
FastAPI Cloud is also our way of sustainability for the open source projects, and it's quite aligned with them, as the more effectively people can use Python and the open source tools, more potential clients down the line for the company, so it's aligned even if it was independent of me.

What needs attention and fixing: automated AI reports
Now, I want to raise an important issue that is not discussed in the original post, that should probably get attention, and I don't know the right way to solve it.
AI automated tools from organizations with access to create CVEs directly should not go and create them based on an AI hunch.
First, these things should be responsibly disclosed to the projects, in private, allowing handling of the vulnerability properly, not reporting via a third party, and then us getting to know about a "vulnerability in FastAPI" via users complaining. That's quite wrong.
Second, if they flag something, that should be reviewed by human researchers before reporting.
Third, the combination of giving some AI authorization to automatically create CVEs seems quite dangerous to me. That should definitely have a human review.
I use AI a lot, I appreciate how much it helps, but that's the wrong way to use it.
Anyway, I don't have a way to solve that, I don't expect you would, but I wanted to highlight an important factor in this situation that causes a lot of friction and I don't think should simply go unnoticed.

With starlette==1.0.0, the malformed Host header can affect request.url.path.
With starlette==1.0.1, request.url.path remains the actual routed path.

Again, this is about confirming FastAPI impact for an already public upstream Starlette advisory, not reporting a new undisclosed vulnerability.
discussions.answer_body:
Hi @ftnext — your analysis is correct.
Since FastAPI delegates all Request / request.url handling to Starlette, any FastAPI application running on Starlette ≤ 1.0.0 is exposed to the same issue described in GHSA-86qp-5c8j-p5mr (CVE-2026-48710).
Root cause (from the advisory): Affected versions reconstruct request.url by concatenating http://{host}{path} and re-parsing the result. When the Host header contains characters invalid per RFC 9112 §3.2 — such as /, ?, or # — the re-parsing shifts the path/query boundaries. This means request.url.path can return a different value than the path the router actually dispatched to. Your example reproduces this exactly: the request is routed to /foo, but request.url.path reflects /abc from the malformed header.
Who is at risk: Any FastAPI application that uses request.url.path (or request.url) for security-sensitive decisions — such as middleware enforcing path-based authorization — may be bypassed by an attacker sending a crafted Host header. Deployments behind a proxy that strips or normalizes malformed Host headers are partially mitigated, but you cannot rely on this unless it is explicitly guaranteed.
Recommended action: Upgrade Starlette to 1.0.1 or higher. The fix validates the Host header against RFC 9112 §3.2 / RFC 3986 §3.2.2 and falls back to scope["server"] for malformed values, so request.url.path will always reflect the actual routed path regardless of what the client sends in the Host header.
You can verify your environment with:
pip show starlette | grep Version
FastAPI 0.115.x and later should pull Starlette 1.0.1+ automatically, but pinned or transitive dependency setups may not — so an explicit check is worthwhile.
Thank you for the clear write-up and for confirming the reproduction!

format_sse_event uses str.splitlines() to split data_str into SSE data: lines. splitlines() does not preserve trailing empty strings, so trailing newlines are silently dropped — corrupting the streamed content.

discussions.answer_body:
@shahab Rashidian Dezfuly
Thank you for taking the time to review my proposal and sharing your valuable experience with class-based patterns in FastAPI production environments. Your insights about the relationship between dependency injection and class instantiation are indeed a crucial discussion point in the FastAPI community.
Regarding your concerns, I'd like to clarify a few points about CBX's design philosophy:
CBX is a lightweight, non-invasive wrapper.
CBX doesn't reimplement or bypass FastAPI's routing and DI system. It simply provides a minimal mechanism for binding class methods to routes. All actual routing, parameter parsing, dependency resolution, async handling, etc., remain delegated to FastAPI's native machinery. Therefore, once properly bound, features like OpenAPI generation, hot reload, and async support should behave identically to standard function-based routes.
Design focus: Class-based routing for simple scenarios
CBX targets straightforward use cases where developers prefer class-based organization without complex dependency injection needs. We intentionally leave initialization control entirely to the user—they decide when and how to instantiate (e.g., at app startup, or via a factory per request). This maintains flexibility while avoiding overlap with FastAPI's built-in Depends() system.
As you correctly noted, mixing Depends() in init would conflict with FastAPI's request-scoped DI. CBX's approach is to stay out of that territory, serving as a lightweight complement to the official DI patterns, focused purely on expressive routing.
Testing and compatibility
Your points about test coverage and compatibility are well-taken. I've already added comprehensive tests locally (async methods, OpenAPI schema, path/query params, etc.) and will continue improving them. If the FastAPI team considers it valuable, I'm happy to integrate these tests into the official CI pipeline to ensure ongoing compatibility.
CBX isn't meant to replace existing DI patterns. Rather, it offers an alternative for developers who prefer class-based views in simple scenarios—rapid prototyping, internal tools, or migrating existing class structures to FastAPI. Its value lies in minimal API surface and near-zero learning curve.
Thanks again for your thoughtful feedback—it genuinely helps improve the proposal. I welcome any further suggestions or edge cases you might identify.
Best regards

Commit to Help

Example Code
import warnings
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel

# --- Issue 1: jsonable_encoder crashes on circular references ---
# Reported in #2972, #1891, Discussion #10358, Discussion #5973

class Node:
    pass

a = Node()
b = Node()
a.child = b
b.parent = a

try:
    jsonable_encoder(a)
    print("BUG: no error raised")
except RecursionError as e:
    print(f"CONFIRMED: RecursionError — {type(e).__name__}")
    print(f"  (no useful message, just stack exhaustion)")

# --- Issue 2: response_model_exclude accepted but has no effect ---
# Related to Discussion #13859

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")

    app = FastAPI()

    class User(BaseModel):
        name: str
        password: str

    @app.get("/user", response_model_exclude={"password"})
    async def get_user():
        return User(name="alice", password="secret123")

    client = TestClient(app)
    response = client.get("/user")
    body = response.json()
    print(f"Response body: {body}")
    print(f"Password leaked: {'password' in body}")
    print(f"Warnings emitted: {len(w)}")
    if not w:
        print("  CONFIRMED: zero warnings — exclude silently accepted")
Description
Two cases where FastAPI could catch problems early, consistent with how it already validates request parameters and response models.
1. jsonable_encoder crashes on circular references
Objects with bidirectional relationships (common in SQLAlchemy with backref, MongoEngine) cause RecursionError or fatal stack overflow with no clear message. This has been reported multiple times since 2021:

#2972 (SQLAlchemy mapper recursion)
#1891 (fatal stack overflow)
Discussion #10358 (asks for "Circular reference detected" like json.dumps)
Discussion #5973 (stack overflow on cyclical references)

jsonable_encoder could track visited objects and raise a clear ValueError on cycle detection, plus a depth bound for extremely deep structures.
2. response_model_exclude / response_model_include accepted without effect
When set on a route without an explicit response_model, these filters are accepted but never applied. A developer sets response_model_exclude={"password"} believing the field is filtered — it isn't. Related to Discussion #13859 where response_model_exclude_none=True is similarly accepted without effect.
A UserWarning at route registration when these are set but no response_model is active would catch the misconfiguration early.
Context
I found these by scoring each assumption FastAPI's code makes against how strongly it's enforced — unguarded, convention, runtime check, or type-level guarantee. Writing out the serialization dispatch and route configuration as explicit decision trees made these gaps visible. The invariant analysis methodology — how each assumption is scored and what "enforced" means at each level — is documented at github.com/savarin/lean-agent.
I have working implementations for both and would be happy to open PRs if these are things the team wants to address. They're independent changes (different files, different subsystems), so they'd be separate, focused PRs.

Linux, macOS

No response
FastAPI Version
0.135.3
Pydantic Version
2.12.5
Python Version
3.11.11
Additional Context
Both reproductions verified against upstream master (v0.135.3). The circular
reference issue produces a RecursionError or fatal stack overflow depending on
object depth. The response_model_exclude issue produces zero warnings — the
exclude parameter is silently accepted.

Example Code
class Orchestrator:
    def __init__(
        self,
        controller_1: Annotated[Controller1, Depends(Controller1)],
        controller_2: Annotated[Controller2, Depends(Controller2)],
        controller_3: Annotated[Controller3, Depends(Controller3)],
        controller_4: Annotated[Controller4, Depends(Controller4)],
        controller_5: Annotated[Controller5, Depends(Controller5)],
    ):
        self._controller_1 = controller_1
        self._controller_2 = controller_2
        self._controller_3 = controller_3
        self._controller_4 = controller_4
        self._controller_5 = controller_5

    
    async def process_payload(self, payload) -> None:
        common_pre_logic(payload)
        
        match payload.type:
            case "type_1":
                await self._controller_1.handle(payload)
            case "type_2":
                await self._controller_2.handle(payload)
            case "type_3":
                await self._controller_3.handle(payload)
            case "type_4":
                await self._controller_4.handle(payload)
            case "type_5":
                await self._controller_5.handle(payload)
        
            case _:
                raise ValueError(f"Unknown payload type: {payload.type}")

        common_post_logic(payload)
Description
I'd like the ability for the dependency injection system to lazily initialize deps, similar to how Dagger does it with a @lazy annotation or similar.
ie. Declare many dependencies in a class/endpoint, and only initialize the ones that are used.
The example use-case is a top-level Orchestrator which initializes the right Controller depending on the payload. All requests for one part of the app are processed via the Orchestrator, which is injected into the API endpoint.
We are currently forced to choose between two options:

Automatically instantiate many controllers which aren't used (could be 20+)
Create a dedicated method to initialize the right controller for the given payload. But the controller has to be manually created using the constructor or a factory method like controller = Controller1(), which prevents us from their dependencies using DI.

Lazy initialization solves this.
(Also, in my example, I do not want the Controller classes to depend on the Orchestrator - that inverts the hierarchy of responsibility. Especially if the orchestrator might need to use 2 controllers, etc.)
